title: Query cost of reducing testing adaptivity
formal: For testing an arbitrary Boolean property, how much can the universal query bound improve when a k-round-adaptive tester is replaced by an \(\ell\)-round-adaptive tester, with \(0\le \ell <k\)? Writing \(q_{j}\) for the minimum query complexity at the same input length and proximity parameter, the source asks for a bound \(q_{\ell}\le \varphi (q_{k},\ell ,k)\) better than the general simulation \(q_{\ell}\le 2^{q_{k}}- 1\) when \(\ell >0\). A one-round reduction \(q_{k- 1}\le q_{k}(1+2^{q_{k}/k})\) is already proved. The source does not specify the amount or regime of improvement required of a general \(\varphi\), so the quantitative target remains unfinished.
context:
A batch allows parallel access to many input positions. Reducing the number of batches may require more queries because later choices can no longer use as much information from earlier answers.

Proposition 26 supplies a universal cost for deleting one round. Open Problem 3 asks for a more general dependence on the number of rounds retained, and the preceding remark keeps batch sizes adaptive.

The institutional record links the 2018 journal publication, but its downloaded attachment uses the conference layout and repeats the same broad open question. It does not justify claiming that the full journal text or a later quantitative resolution was checked.
why: Quantifies the general price of replacing sequential information gathering by fewer batches. A substantive universal bound would apply across Boolean property testing, beyond the behavior of one particular property.

importance.reason: A general resource tradeoff for adaptive Boolean property testing; a precise quantitative target is needed to distinguish a substantive advance from the existing simulations. Existing score retained.

sentences: The source asks how query complexity changes when a tester is allowed fewer batches of queries.
Its convention counts k rounds of adaptivity as \(k+1\) actual batches.
A general exponential simulation and a better bound for removing one round are already known.
The requested new bound must cover arbitrary properties and allow the number of queries in each batch to depend on earlier answers.
The source leaves the amount and asymptotic regime of the desired improvement unspecified, which this card records explicitly.

definitions:
Fix an integer \(n\ge 1, a\) nonempty property \(\mathrm{P}\subseteq \{0,1\}^{n}\), and a proximity parameter \(\varepsilon \in\)(0,1]. An input \(f:[n]\to \{0,1\}\) is available through a value oracle: a query i returns the single bit \(f(i)\). Its distance from P is \(\min _{g\in \mathrm{P}}|\{i:f(i)\ne g(i)\}|/n\). The tester must accept every \(f\in \mathrm{P}\) with probability at least \(2/3\), and reject every input at distance strictly greater than \(\varepsilon\) with probability at least \(2/3\). On other inputs either verdict is allowed. Probabilities are over the tester’s internal random bits. This is ordinary two-sided testing with uniform Hamming distance, not tolerant testing, distribution testing or sample-only access.

Under the source’s convention, j rounds of adaptivity mean \(j+1\) batches \(Q_{0},\ldots ,Q_{j}\). Each batch is chosen using internal randomness and the answers to all earlier batches. All locations in the current batch must be chosen before any of its answers are revealed. Batches may be empty. Both the identities of locations and the number of queries in a later batch may depend on earlier answers. Thus \(j=0\) is a fully nonadaptive tester with one batch; \(j=1\) permits two batches. The total number of value queries, summed over all batches and bounded on every input and random tape, is the cost. Local computation, descriptions of the property and query addresses are not charged as additional queries. Duplicate queries can be avoided or answered from stored values.

For this fixed \(n,\mathrm{P},\varepsilon\), let \(q_{j}(n,\mathrm{P},\varepsilon )\) be the smallest worst-case number of queries used by a j-round-adaptive tester satisfying those guarantees. Algorithms are nonuniform in the source: for each n and known property they may be chosen separately. No polynomial running-time or uniform construction of testers from a succinct property description is required. Query budgets can always be capped at n by reading the entire input; extra empty rounds are harmless. The desired bound is universal over these Boolean properties and uses the same \(\varepsilon\) on both sides. Its function \(\varphi\) is to depend only on \(q_{k},\ell ,k\), with \(n,\mathrm{P},\varepsilon\) entering only through \(q_{k}\).

Section 6.1 proves \(q_{k}\le q_{\ell}\le 2^{q_{k}}- 1\) for \(0\le \ell \le k\) and \(q_{k- 1}\le q_{k}(1+2^{q_{k}/k})\) for \(k>0\). The first exponent is \(q_{k}\); it is not the linear expression \(2q_{k}- 1\). These are known universal upper bounds, not the unanswered result. Iterating the one-round inequality also supplies a bound for several removed rounds; the source’s wording does not select an explicit quantitative improvement over that consequence. Its remark stresses that general testers can adapt their batch sizes, so a theorem assuming a predetermined size for each batch would address only a special case.

The remaining task is to specify which joint regime of \(q_{k},k,\ell\) is being compared and what counts as a sufficient asymptotic improvement. The source does not demand matching lower bounds for an extremal tradeoff function, nor does it state a particular exponent-saving conjecture. This card therefore does not certify either of those stronger replacements.
answer_criterion: A completed statement must specify the asymptotic upper bound \(\varphi\) and the regime and precision in which it improves the known simulation. A valid universal result must preserve the property, proximity parameter, success probability, adaptive batch-size freedom and worst-case query convention. The existing one-round theorem alone is not new progress; an optimal upper-and-lower tradeoff would be a stronger task than the source explicitly states.
